newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-NEW CHARTER TO COMBAT PREDICTABILITY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NEW CHARTER TO COMBAT PREDICTABILITY.

text.p: Rugby union lawmakers have drafted a charter to combat the growing predictability of the game -- particularly in the southern hemisphere.
The technical committee of the International Rugby Football Board (IRFB) released the five-page document at the end of a four-day meeting in Cape Town on Friday.
The charter explains the principles of the game and how the laws should be interpreted by referees.

Syd Millar of Ireland, chairman of the committee, said: "We felt that the game had become a little bit predictable in that there was no longer a fair contest for possession anymore. You had situations where a team would retain the ball for 12 or 14 phases because there was no fair contest for possession.
"It annoys me to see a member of a defending team going to play the ball only to be told by a match official to get away.
"It's gone a bit too far in the Super 12."
Millar said there was no need to alter the laws. What needed to be altered was the approach of referees, coaches and players.
Videos are to be produced explaining how each aspect of the game should be interpreted in the pursuit of consistent refereeing worldwide.
The charter will be sent to each of the 74 member unions of the IRFB and then to individual clubs and provinces.
However Millar wants referees to act immediately on the charter.
Millar said: "The laws tell you what you can't do but there's nothing written down on how the game should be played."
He said scrums and line-outs had also become token contests as the crooked feed at both was being overlooked by referees.
This year's Super 12 produced the usual feast of tries with Auckland retaining the title in an unusually low-scoring match against the ACT Brumbies, winning 23-7.
"Most of the Super 12 is admirable. We just feel that it has gone a little on the predictable side," said Millar.
